## 3. CLEAR ICE BLOCK — THE BINDING CONSTRAINT

### 3a. Clinebell directional-freezing block makers

**Clinebell Equipment Co.**, Loveland, Colorado, USA — `clinebellequipment.com` [R, blocked this session]. The industry standard for crystal-clear block ice; the entire American ice-carving and craft-cocktail industry runs on these.

| Spec | Value | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| Model | **CB300X2** — produces **two** blocks per cycle | [R] |
| Block size | **~10" × 20" × 40"** (250 × 500 × 1,000 mm) | [R] |
| Block weight | **300 lb / 136 kg** each | [R] |
| Cycle time | **~3.5–4 days** | [R] |
| Method | Directional freezing — freezes bottom-up with circulating pumps that carry dissolved air and impurities upward, leaving optically clear ice | [ENG] — this is the physics, and it is why you cannot substitute a normal freezer |
| Electrical | ~1.1–1.5 kW continuous, 115 V or 230 V | [R] |
| **New price** | **$12,000–19,000 ex-works Colorado** | **[R] — low confidence, verify** |
| **Landed Baghdad** | **$16,000–24,000** | [E] |
| **Used** | **$6,000–10,000** (ice-carving trade channels) | [R] |

Clinebell also lists larger units (**CB405** and similar) producing more/larger blocks. **I could not verify the model designations or output of anything above the CB300X2 and I am not confident enough to quote them.** Ask the factory directly.

### 3b. ⚠️ THE YIELD CALCULATION — the most important number in this report [ENG]

```
CB300X2 output    = 2 blocks × 136.1 kg ÷ 3.75-day cycle = 72.6 kg clear ice / day

Al-Qalab vessel:  ~110 × 110 × 130 mm billet = 1.57 L = 1.44 kg gross ice
                  less ~250 ml drink cavity  → ~1.20 kg finished vessel
Saw kerf + squaring the block + carving waste = 30–40%
                  → 1.7–2.4 kg of block ice consumed per vessel

CAPACITY PER MACHINE = 72.6 ÷ 1.7…2.4 = 30–42 vessels/day  (call it 35)
```

Now overlay the existing financial model [MODEL]:

| Scenario | Transactions/day | Items/day (×1.45) | Al-Qalab @ 5.45% unit share | Utilisation of ONE CB300X2 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Mature annual average | 300 | 435 | **24 / day** | **62–70%** |
| Peak summer month | 440 | 638 | **35 / day** | **90–100% — AT CAPACITY** |

**Findings:**

1. **The model's revenue mix is physically achievable — but only just, and only in the annual average.** The decision to cap Al-Qalab at 12% of revenue was correct and is now quantitatively justified: **the binding constraint is 30–42 carved vessels per day per machine.** Put that number in the deck. It is the kind of specificity that makes an investor believe the operator has actually thought about the product.
2. **One machine is a single point of failure on the hero SKU.** A compressor failure costs you a minimum of **4 days** (the freeze cycle) *even after the repair is done* — plus repair lead time in a country with **no Clinebell service agent and no spare-parts channel**. In peak summer that is ~$1,400–2,400 of lost Al-Qalab revenue plus incalculable brand damage on the product the whole concept is named around.
3. **Recommendation: budget a second machine (+$16–20k), OR make scarcity the policy.** The second option is cheaper *and* better marketing: *"40 blocks carved daily. When they're gone, they're gone."* A daily sell-out on the signature item is a queue generator, not a failure. But it must be a deliberate, stated strategy in the deck — not something an investor discovers by doing this arithmetic themselves.
4. **The model's `clear_ice_system: 34000`** [MODEL] is consistent with one Clinebell + saw + drill + carving tools + RO train ($28.5k in my BASE) with ~$5k of headroom. **Line broadly validated for a one-machine build.** It does *not* contain a second machine.

### 3c. Chinese / Turkish alternatives

Chinese "block ice machines" are overwhelmingly **brine-tank plants producing CLOUDY block ice** for fish and produce cooling — 1–5 tonne/day, $10,000–60,000. **These are the wrong product.** Cloudy ice is not a food-presentation material and it is not made from potable water.

A minority of Chinese suppliers list "**transparent block ice machine**" using directional freezing, typically 100–300 kg/day: **$3,000–9,000 FOB** [R, low confidence]. Suppliers to check: **Focusun** (Shanghai Focusun Refrigeration, `focusun.com`), **CBFI / Guangzhou Icesource** (`cbfi.com`), **Koller** (`kollerchina.com`). Verify clarity with sample photographs *of ice cut and back-lit*, not marketing renders — this is where these suppliers most often disappoint.

### 3d. Buying blocks instead of making them

| Market | 300 lb / 136 kg crystal-clear block | Tag |
|---|---|---|
| USA (ice-carving supplier) | **$100–175** | [R] |
| **Dubai / Gulf** (ice sculpture companies) | **AED 400–900 ≈ $110–245** | [E] — derived from typical Gulf ice-sculpture pricing; verify with Dubai suppliers |
| **Baghdad** | **NO KNOWN SUPPLIER** | [E] |

**This is a strategically important finding.** Baghdad ice plants sell cloudy 25 kg block ice at roughly 500–1,000 IQD ($0.35–0.70) — made for *cooling fish and produce*, from municipal water, in facilities with no food-grade certification. Cross-reference the sibling market report's finding that **most urban Baghdad residents will not drink tap water** because of Tigris contamination. **You cannot serve local block ice as food.** SHABM must produce its own clear ice from RO water. That is not an optional capex line — it is a food-safety requirement, and it converts the Clinebell from "nice-to-have theatre" into "licence to operate."

**Corollary — a real, un-modelled revenue line.** If SHABM installs the first directional-freezing clear-ice capability in Iraq, it also becomes the *only* supplier of crystal-clear cocktail ice and ice sculpture to Baghdad's hotels, embassies and event market. That is a B2B wholesale business sitting on top of already-purchased equipment, and it changes the payback maths on a second machine. **Worth a line in the deck; it is currently absent from the financial model.**

### 3e. Making an ice CUP — is there a machine? [ENG]

**Short answer: no off-the-shelf machine does this. The engineered process is a three-step line, and it is cheap.**

There is no commercial "ice cup driller" product I can identify. What exists:

- **Japanese ice-ball presses** — heated/gravity aluminium dies that melt a sphere out of an ice cube. **Cocktail Kingdom** press ~$1,000–1,300; **Taisin** (Japan) ~$800–1,500 [R]. These prove the *principle*: **a heated metal form sinks into ice and leaves a perfect cavity.** They do not make cups.
- **Silicone/plastic "ice shot glass" moulds** — $10–40. But these freeze *outward from all sides*, producing **cloudy** ice. Wrong product for a hero SKU.
- **CNC ice routers** — these exist (ice companies use them for logos), but I could not verify a vendor or price. **[E] $20,000–70,000.** The practical DIY equivalent is a 3-axis CNC router ($6,000–15,000) inside a −10 °C cold room ($6,000–14,000) with a cold-tolerant spindle and chip evacuation. **Only justified at GCC flagship scale — it is in my HIGH column, not BASE.**

**The recommended process line (BASE case, ~$8,500 all-in):**

| Step | Equipment | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| 1. Produce | Clinebell CB300X2 from RO water | $16,000 | 136 kg blocks, 72.6 kg/day |
| 2. Temper | Rest block at −5 °C for 6–12 h | (cold room / freezer) | **Critical.** Ice straight from −10 °C shatters when cut. Untempered ice is the #1 cause of waste in carving. |
| 3. Section | Ice bandsaw → 110 mm billets | $4,000 | A 16–20" meat bandsaw with a stainless/food-grade blade works |
| 4. Bore cavity | **Heated aluminium cup die** (custom): ~100 mm Ø × 130 mm deep machined form + cartridge heaters + PID + press frame | **$1,500–4,000** | This is a local machine-shop fabrication job, not a purchase. Sinks a smooth, optically clear cavity in 30–90 s. |
| 5. Finish | Hand tools, torch polish, tongs, cut-resistant gloves | $1,500 | |

Cheapest possible route: a **drill press + 90 mm diamond core bit** ($200–600) bores the cavity mechanically. Faster to set up, rougher finish, more waste. Fine for prototyping the recipe; not for a hero SKU at $9.80.

## 4. ULTRA-LOW TEMPERATURE (−80 °C) FREEZERS

### ⚠️ 4a. THE AMBIENT-TEMPERATURE PROBLEM — this will kill the −80 line if unaddressed

**Every major ULT manufacturer rates their freezers to a maximum ambient of ~30–32 °C** [R, high confidence — this is a consistent industry-wide spec]:

| Manufacturer | Model family | Rated operating ambient |
|---|---|---|
| Thermo Fisher Scientific | TSX / TDE series | **15–32 °C** |
| Eppendorf | CryoCube F740 | **16–32 °C** |
| Haier Biomedical | DW-86L series | **10–32 °C** |
| PHCbi (ex-Panasonic) | MDF-DU series | **5–30 °C** |

**Baghdad summer ambient is 45–50 °C outdoors and, in an unconditioned commercial back-of-house, routinely 38–45 °C.**

A cascade ULT refrigeration system operating 13–18 °C above its rated ambient will:
- fail to reach or hold −80 °C (the second-stage cascade cannot reject heat),
- run the first-stage compressor continuously at high discharge pressure → **thermal trip, then compressor failure**,
- **void the warranty** — every manufacturer excludes out-of-spec ambient operation,
- and consume **30–60% more energy** even when it does hold (energy rises ~3–5% per °C of ambient) [E].

**Therefore the ULT freezer requires a dedicated, continuously conditioned, insulated closet held at ≤ 25 °C, with redundant cooling and generator backup.** This is a **$2,500–10,000 CAPEX line that does not appear in most equipment quotes** and which I suspect is not inside the model's `ult_cold_chain: 16000` [MODEL].

Additional design requirement [ENG]: a ULT freezer rejects **0.7–1.5 kW continuously** and up to **~2.5 kW during pull-down**. In a small closet that is a self-defeating heat load. **Either duct the condenser heat outside, or specify a water-cooled-condenser ULT variant** (Thermo and PHCbi both offer them) — the water-cooled option is materially better engineering for this climate and should be the specified default.

Over 7 years that is $4,300 — meaningful but *not* enough on its own to justify a $14,000 price premium. **Buy the Haier for economics; buy the Thermo for warranty support and resale.** [E]

### 4c. ⚠️ Right-sizing — a genuine CAPEX saving

**How many cups actually need to be at −80 °C simultaneously?** [ENG]

A pre-frozen vessel handed to a customer in 45 °C air loses its visible frost/vapour effect in **1–3 minutes**. The theatre is in the *hand-off*, not in storage duration. At the model's peak of ~163 Saqee'-80 units/day over a 15-hour day, you need perhaps **20–40 cups in the ULT at any moment**, not 300.

**A 100–200 L chest ULT ($3,500–6,000) is likely sufficient**, and a chest form factor is *strictly better* in this application than an upright: it loses far less cold air on opening, has better thermal inertia through a generator switchover, and tolerates a higher ambient in practice. **Potential saving vs a 578 L upright: $4,000–6,000.** Prototype the actual cup turnover before buying the big unit.

### 4d. Two safety/spec points that belong in the equipment brief [ENG]

1. **A −80 °C vessel is a contact-burn hazard.** Bare skin adheres to metal at −80 °C. The cup **must** be double-wall stainless with an insulating sleeve or holder, served with tongs, and staff must be trained. This is a product-design and liability requirement, not an afterthought.
2. **Thermal shock.** Pouring espresso and milk into a ceramic or glass vessel at −80 °C will crack it. **Specify double-wall stainless.** The model's COGS note already lists "faceted double-wall cup" at $0.42 [MODEL] — **correct, keep it.**

### 8c. ⚠️ Cooling a glass box in 50 °C — full load calculation [ENG]

Assumptions: 25 m² footprint, 3.0 m high, ~45 m² glazed, outdoor design **50 °C**, indoor **24 °C** (ΔT = 26 K), 15 occupants, 4 ACH infiltration (high-traffic door), all refrigeration condensers **ducted outside**.

| Load component | Calculation | Watts |
|---|---|---:|
| Glass conduction | 45 m² × 1.7 W/m²K × 26 K | 1,989 |
| Solar gain | 20 m² sunlit × 700 W/m² × SHGC 0.35 | 4,900 |
| Roof | 25 m² × 0.35 × (78−24) sol-air | 472 |
| Infiltration/door | 4 ACH × 75 m³ → 0.083 m³/s × 1.2 × 1005 × 26 | 2,613 |
| Occupants | 15 × (75 sensible + 55 latent) | 1,950 |
| Lighting + IT | 25 m² × 20 W/m² + 300 | 800 |
| Equipment residual (boilers, cabinet losses) | — | 2,700 |
| **TOTAL** | | **15,424 W = 15.4 kW = 4.39 TR** |
| **+15% margin → design load** | | **5.0 TR** |
| **If condensers are INSIDE (+9 kW)** | | **6.9 TR** |

**Findings:**

1. **Specify 5–6 TR for a 25 m² glass kiosk.** That is **~0.22 TR/m²**, versus ~0.08–0.10 TR/m² for a normal café — **more than double**. That premium is the direct, quantifiable cost of the "giant ice cube" brand concept. It is defensible, but it must be named in the deck before an investor names it for you.
2. **Duct every refrigeration condenser outside.** Leaving them indoors adds 9 kW and pushes you to 7 TR — a ~40% increase in both AC capex and AC running cost, forever.
3. **⚠️ Specify T3-rated ("tropical", rated to 52 °C) units — Gree, Midea, Daikin Tropical, Carrier Gulf-spec, LG.** A standard T1 unit is rated at 35 °C outdoor. At 50 °C it loses 25–35% capacity and will trip on high head pressure at 2pm in July. T3 units are the regional norm in Iraq and the Gulf; the failure mode is a contractor quietly substituting T1 to win the tender.
4. **Solar is the largest single load (4.9 kW, 32%).** A frosted/textured acrylic skin acting as a diffuser, plus external shading or a low-SHGC low-e glass spec, can cut this by 30–40% — the cheapest kW you will ever remove. **Coordinate the façade spec with the HVAC spec.** These are usually two different consultants who never speak.

**Equipment cost** [E]: T3 ducted split, 3 TR: $1,200–2,200 (Gree/Midea class) or $2,500–4,500 (Daikin/Carrier/LG). Two 3 TR units for N+1 partial redundancy + ductwork + electrical: **$5,000–14,000 installed**.

**Running cost** [ENG]: 6 TR = 21 kW cooling; EER degrades to ~2.2–2.8 W/W at 50 °C → **7.5–9.5 kW electrical**; × 14 h/day = **105–133 kWh/day for AC alone**.
